planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall before the ground freezes, or set out container-grown plants in spring, in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full to part sun.

directions: All the Buzz forms rounded, globe-shaped flower clusters held on sturdy stems above a low tuft of strap-like foliage, blooming through summer and drawing in bees and other pollinators by the dozen. Plant it in well-drained soil of average fertility and give it a spot with at least four hours of direct sun daily. Once established the clumps tolerate dry spells with ease and shrug off deer and rabbit browsing, making this a low-fuss choice for borders and pollinator plantings. Leave the foliage in place until it yellows naturally so the bulbs can recharge for next year's bloom.

common_name: Sun Jewels Rubies and Diamonds Fern-Leaved Bleeding Heart
scientific_name: Dicentra hybrid 'Sun Jewels Rubies and Diamonds'

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in sharply drained, average soil in full sun to part shade; avoid heavy, wet clay.

directions: Unlike the shade-loving woodland bleeding hearts most gardeners know, this alpine-type selection carries ferny, blue-green foliage and sprays of ruby-red and white bicolor flowers that keep opening from spring clear through fall in full sun to part shade. Give it sharply drained soil, since the plant sulks and rots in heavy clay or standing moisture. Established plants attract bees and hummingbirds while resisting deer, and the long bloom window makes it a reliable front-of-border filler well beyond the usual spring-only bleeding heart display. Avoid overwatering, especially in winter.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this spreading ground cover resents rich, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Cloud Cover smothers itself in small white, five-petaled flowers over a low, spreading mat of silvery, felted foliage, peaking in late spring but continuing sporadically into fall. It thrives in poor, lean, well-drained soil and needs almost no supplemental water once rooted in, making it a workhorse for hot, dry banks, rock gardens, and between stepping stones. Shear the mat back lightly after the main flush of bloom to keep the foliage tight and encourage a tidier regrowth. Avoid fertile, moisture-retentive soil, which causes the mat to open up and rot at the center.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in lean, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun; avoid hard fall pruning into old wood.

directions: One of the earliest English lavenders to show color each season, Summer Serenade pushes up dense spikes of fragrant purple-blue flowers above tidy, silvery foliage from early into late summer. Plant it in lean, well-drained soil with neutral to alkaline pH and full sun, since rich or soggy ground shortens its life considerably. Once settled, the compact mounds tolerate heat and drought with ease, draw in bees and butterflies, and shrug off deer and rabbits. Skip hard pruning into the woody base in fall; light shaping right after bloom is enough to keep the plant tidy.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; part of the Prairie Winds native grass series.

directions: Blue Steel is a native big bluestem selection prized for its strongly upright, steely blue-green foliage that stays clean through summer before turning coppery-bronze in fall. Airy, fine-textured flower panicles rise above the clump in late summer and persist as winter interest once cut back is delayed until late winter. It handles average to poor, well-drained soil and extended dry spells without flinching, needing no staking or fertilizer to perform. Use it as a vertical accent or screen in prairie-style and native plantings where its narrow, non-flopping habit earns its keep.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; part of the Prairie Winds native grass series, best suited to warmer zones.

directions: Candy Floss erupts into billowing clouds of cotton-candy pink flower panicles above fine, airy foliage in late summer and fall, creating one of the most photogenic displays among ornamental grasses. It wants full sun and well-drained soil, and once established it shrugs off heat and drought with minimal care. The wide, arching mound works well massed along walkways or borders where its pink haze can be backlit by low afternoon sun. Cut the whole clump back hard in late winter to make room for fresh spring growth before the pink plumes return the following fall.
